questions.stem:
A vertical tower of height \(h\) metres stands with its base at a point \(O\) on horizonal ground. At the same instant, stone A is projected from \(O\) with speed \(V\ \text{ms}^{-1}\) at an angle \(\alpha\) above the horizontal and stone B is projected from the top of the tower with speed \(U\ \text{ms}^{-1}\) at an angle \(\beta\) above the horizontal, where \(\alpha\gt\beta\). The two stones move in the same vertical plane under gravity, where the acceleration due to gravity is \(g\ \text{ms}^{-2}\), and collide after \(T\) seconds. At time t seconds after firing, the position vectors of the two stones are

\(\mathbf{r}_A(t)=(Vt\cos\alpha)\mathbf{i}+\left(-\frac12gt^2+Vt\sin\alpha\right)\mathbf{j}\)
\(\mathbf{r}_B(t)=(Ut\cos\beta)\mathbf{i}+\left(h-\frac12gt^2+Ut\sin\beta\right)\mathbf{j}\) . (DO NOT PROVE THIS)

Show that \(T=\frac{h\cos\alpha}{U\sin(\alpha-\beta)}\) .
questions.hint: Equate the i and j components at time T, then eliminate V.

steps.explain: They collide at time \(T\), so the position vectors are equal. Equate the \(\mathbf{i}\) components and cancel \(T\).
Equate the \(\mathbf{j}\) components; the \(-\frac12gT^2\) terms cancel.
Eliminate \(V\). Multiply (1) by \(T\sin\alpha\).
Multiply (2) by \(\cos\alpha\).
The left sides of (3) and (4) are equal, so the right sides are equal.
Use \(\sin\alpha\cos\beta-\cos\alpha\sin\beta=\sin(\alpha-\beta)\) and solve for \(T\).

meta.source: Caringbah 2020 3U Trials & Solutions

questions.answer: At T, r_A = r_B. i: \(V\cos\alpha=U\cos\beta\) (1). j: \(VT\sin\alpha=h+UT\sin\beta\) (2). (1)×T sin α: \(VT\sin\alpha\cos\alpha=UT\cos\beta\sin\alpha\). (2)×cos α: \(VT\sin\alpha\cos\alpha=h\cos\alpha+UT\sin\beta\cos\alpha\). Subtract: \(UT(\sin\alpha\cos\beta-\cos\alpha\sin\beta)=h\cos\alpha\), i.e. \(UT\sin(\alpha-\beta)=h\cos\alpha\), so \(T=\frac{h\cos\alpha}{U\sin(\alpha-\beta)}\).

keyPoints.note: At the collision r_A(T) = r_B(T): two equations, one from i and one from j.

questions.stem: A rock is projected with a speed of \(V\ \text{m\,s}^{-1}\) from a point \(4\) metres above a flat ground. The angle of projection to the horizontal is \(\theta\) as shown. Taking the ground as the origin and the acceleration due to gravity as \(10\ \text{m\,s}^{-2}\), show that \(x=Vt\cos\theta\) and \(y=Vt\sin\theta-5t^{2}+4\). Which derivation is correct?
questions.hint: Integrate the acceleration twice, using the initial conditions at \(t=0\): velocity components \(V\cos\theta\) (horizontal) and \(V\sin\theta\) (vertical), position \((0,4)\).

steps.explain: Initial velocity components (green and red in the figure).

Horizontal: no horizontal force, so \(\ddot{x}=0\). Integrate: \(\dot{x}=C_{1}\); at \(t=0\), \(\dot{x}=V\cos\theta\), so \(C_{1}=V\cos\theta\). Integrate again: \(x=Vt\cos\theta+C_{2}\); \(x(0)=0\Rightarrow C_{2}=0\).
Vertical: gravity acts DOWNWARDS: \(\ddot{y}=-10\). Integrate: \(\dot{y}=-10t+C_{1}\); \(\dot{y}(0)=V\sin\theta\Rightarrow C_{1}=V\sin\theta\).
Integrate again: \(y=-5t^{2}+Vt\sin\theta+C_{2}\). The rock starts 4 m above the ground (origin on the ground): \(y(0)=4\Rightarrow C_{2}=4\).
Why not the others: B starts from \(y=0\) (ignores the 4 m); C uses \(9.8\) (the question says \(10\)); D has gravity pointing up (positive acceleration).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Integrate twice; y(0) = 4 gives the constant.

Beginning with its acceleration vector, derive the velocity at any time \(t\) in the form \(\underset{\sim}{v}=\dot{x}\underset{\sim}{i}+\dot{y}\underset{\sim}{j}\).
questions.hint: Velocity is the INTEGRAL of acceleration (with respect to \(t\)), component by component. Each integration gives a constant: find it from the INITIAL velocity \(\underset{\sim}{v}(0)=12\underset{\sim}{i}+5\underset{\sim}{j}\).

steps.explain: Acceleration components: \(\ddot{x}=0\) and \(\ddot{y}=-10\).
Integrate with respect to \(t\) (add a constant each time): \(\int0\,dt=c_{1}\) and \(\int-10\,dt=-10t+c_{2}\).
Initial velocity (\(t=0\)): \(\dot{x}(0)=12\Rightarrow c_{1}=12\); \(\dot{y}(0)=5\Rightarrow c_{2}=5\).
Write the velocity vector.

Check: at \(t=0\), \(\underset{\sim}{v}=12\underset{\sim}{i}+5\underset{\sim}{j}\) ✓; differentiating gives \(0\underset{\sim}{i}-10\underset{\sim}{j}\) ✓. Why not the others: B has \(+10t\) (gravity slows the upward motion); C ignores the initial velocity; D integrates \(-10\) as \(-5t^{2}\) (that is the displacement, not velocity).
So the correct choice is option A.

Golf ball: \(\underset{\sim}{s}=45\sqrt{3}t\underset{\sim}{i}+\left(45t-5t^{2}\right)\underset{\sim}{j}\). Equate the \(\underset{\sim}{j}\) components: \(20-5(t^{2}-10t+25)=45t-5t^{2}\Rightarrow20-5t^{2}+50t-125=45t-5t^{2}\Rightarrow5t=105\Rightarrow t=21\).

Stone: \(\underset{\sim}{s}=Vt\underset{\sim}{i}+\left(20-5t^{2}\right)\underset{\sim}{j}\) (using \(t\) as the stone's own time). Equate \(\underset{\sim}{j}\) components: \(20-5t^{2}=45t-5t^{2}\Rightarrow t=\dfrac{20}{45}=0.44\).
Stone: \(\underset{\sim}{s}=V(t-5)\underset{\sim}{i}+\left(20+5(t-5)^{2}\right)\underset{\sim}{j}\). Equate \(\underset{\sim}{j}\): \(20+5(t-5)^{2}=45t-5t^{2}\), which has no real solution.

Stone: \(\underset{\sim}{s}=V(t-5)\underset{\sim}{i}+\left(20-5(t-5)^{2}\right)\underset{\sim}{j}\). Equate \(\underset{\sim}{i}\) components only: \(V(t-5)=45\sqrt{3}t\), which gives \(t=21\) for every \(V\).
questions.hint: Collision means the SAME position at the SAME time. Measure all times from when the golf ball was hit: the stone has flown for \(t-5\) seconds. Equate the \(\underset{\sim}{j}\) components (they do not involve the unknown \(V\)).

steps.explain: Stone: horizontal launch, so \(\underset{\sim}{v}=V\underset{\sim}{i}-10\tau\underset{\sim}{j}\) and, with \(\tau\) the time since the stone was fired, \(\underset{\sim}{s}=V\tau\underset{\sim}{i}+\left(20-5\tau^{2}\right)\underset{\sim}{j}\) (starting at height 20 m).
The stone is fired 5 s AFTER the golf ball was hit. If \(t\) is the time since the ball was hit, then \(\tau=t-5\).
Collision: positions are equal. Equate the \(\underset{\sim}{j}\)-components of stone and golf ball (the \(\underset{\sim}{i}\)-equation contains the unknown \(V\)).
Solve.
Why not the others: B forgets the 5 s delay; C has the wrong sign for gravity; D uses only the \(\underset{\sim}{i}\) equation (it contains the unknown \(V\) and cannot give \(t\) on its own).
So the correct choice is option A.

Speed \(=|\underset{\sim}{v}|=\sqrt{v_{x}^{2}+v_{y}^{2}}\).
To 3 significant figures: \(190\ \text{m s}^{-1}\). Check: option B is only the horizontal speed \(V\), option C only the vertical component.
So the correct choice is option A.

questions.stem: A rock is projected with a speed of \(V\ \text{m\,s}^{-1}\) from a point \(4\) metres above a flat ground. The angle of projection to the horizontal is \(\theta\) as shown. questions.hint: Eliminate \(t\): from \(x=Vt\cos\theta\) get \(t=\dfrac{x}{V\cos\theta}\), substitute into \(y\). Use \(\tan\theta=\dfrac{5}{12}\) and \(\sec^{2}\theta=1+\tan^{2}\theta\). The rock lands at \(x=30\), \(y=0\).

steps.explain: From \(x=Vt\cos\theta\): \(t=\dfrac{x}{V\cos\theta}\). Substitute into \(y=Vt\sin\theta-5t^{2}+4\).
Use \(\sec^{2}\theta=1+\tan^{2}\theta=1+\dfrac{25}{144}=\dfrac{169}{144}\) and \(\tan\theta=\dfrac{5}{12}\).
Landing point: \(x=30\), \(y=0\).
Square root (\(V>0\)).
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Eliminate t; use x = 30, y = 0 and sec²θ = 1 + tan²θ.

questions.stem: A rock is projected with a speed of \(V\ \text{m\,s}^{-1}\) from a point \(4\) metres above a flat ground. The angle of projection to the horizontal is \(\theta\) as shown. With \(\theta=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{5}{12}\right)\) and \(V=17.89\ \text{m\,s}^{-1}\), find the maximum height reached.
questions.hint: Maximum height occurs when the VERTICAL velocity is 0: \(\dot{y}=0\). Find that time, then substitute it into \(y\). With \(\tan\theta=\dfrac{5}{12}\) the triangle is 5, 12, 13, so \(\sin\theta=\dfrac{5}{13}\).

steps.explain: Triangle with \(\tan\theta=\dfrac{5}{12}\): opposite 5, adjacent 12, hypotenuse \(\sqrt{25+144}=13\).
At the top the rock is moving horizontally: \(\dot{y}=0\).
Substitute this time into \(y=Vt\sin\theta-5t^{2}+4\). First \(V\sin\theta=17.89\times\dfrac{5}{13}=6.881\).
Add.

Check by formula: \(y_{\max}=4+\dfrac{(V\sin\theta)^{2}}{20}=4+\dfrac{47.35}{20}=6.37\) ✓. Why not the others: \(2.37\) forgets the starting height 4 m; \(6.88\) is \(V\sin\theta\) (a velocity); \(12.4\) is an arithmetic slip.
So the correct choice is option A.

keyPoints.note: Max height: set the vertical velocity to zero.

questions.stem: A ball is thrown from the origin \(O\) with a velocity \(V\) and an angle of elevation of \(\theta\), where \(\theta\ne\dfrac{\pi}{2}\). What is the Cartesian equation of the flight path? Take \(g=10\ \mathrm{ms^{-1}}\).
questions.hint: A CARTESIAN equation has only \(x\) and \(y\) (no \(t\)). Start from \(x=Vt\cos\theta\) and \(y=-5t^{2}+Vt\sin\theta\), solve the first for \(t\), substitute into the second, and use \(\dfrac{1}{\cos^{2}\theta}=1+\tan^{2}\theta\).

steps.explain: Acceleration is \(0\) horizontally and \(-g=-10\) vertically. Integrating (starting at the origin) gives the parametric equations.
Eliminate \(t\): from \(x=Vt\cos\theta\) we get \(t=\dfrac{x}{V\cos\theta}\).
Substitute into \(y\).
Use \(\dfrac{1}{\cos^{2}\theta}=\sec^{2}\theta=1+\tan^{2}\theta\).

Why not the others: B uses \(10x^{2}\) (it forgets the \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) in \(\dfrac12gt^{2}\): \(\dfrac{1}{2}\times10=5\)); C and D are PARAMETRIC (they still contain \(t\)), and D also has \(-10t^{2}\) instead of \(-5t^{2}\).
So the correct choice is option A.

They throw a ball from a height of 1.5 metres, at a speed of 5 m/s with an angle of projection of \(40^{\circ}\). The ball just touches the ceiling before landing at the junction of the floor and the wall, as shown. Find the width and height of the room, correct to the nearest centimetre.
